title: Carry Meaning in Small Pieces
learningGoals: Adapt the structure to the listener

deeperExplanation.question: Will using a structure make me sound mechanical?
deeperExplanation.answer: It can if you treat the labels as lines to recite. Try keeping the structure behind the message. Instead of announcing first the what, now the so what, explain the idea, why it matters and a next step in ordinary words. You can omit a part that the listener already knows. The structure serves as support for meaning; the conversation decides how much of it is useful.

sections.narration:
Welcome. Today we are exploring Carry Meaning in Small Pieces. You have several ideas at once. You try to fit them into a single long sentence, lose the thread and start again. You know the topic but cannot find a manageable way to carry it.

In this session, we will find boundaries between ideas, use a small meaning structure, and adapt the structure to the listener. I will explain the idea, show a visual example, and invite you to try it in a small experience of your own. You can ask me a question or switch to reading at any point. We will finish by choosing what, if anything, you want to take into a real conversation.

sections.narration: A meaning piece is one idea the listener can receive before another is added. It might be the main point, a reason, an example or a next step. We will practise separating these pieces without making your speech mechanical. The amount that fits comfortably can change with the topic, language and situation.

sections.narration:
You have several ideas at once. You try to fit them into a single long sentence, lose the thread and start again. You know the topic but cannot find a manageable way to carry it.

A simple structure gives meaning somewhere to go. For an update, try what happened, why it matters and what comes next. For a recommendation, try the problem, a possible solution and its benefit. These are optional supports. You do not have to force every answer into all three parts or remember a formula while someone is speaking.

Will using a structure make me sound mechanical?

It can if you treat the labels as lines to recite. Try keeping the structure behind the message. Instead of announcing first the what, now the so what, explain the idea, why it matters and a next step in ordinary words. You can omit a part that the listener already knows. The structure serves as support for meaning; the conversation decides how much of it is useful.

You can listen back if useful, or reflect without replaying. Changed, unchanged or uncertain experiences are all information.

sections.narration: A pause between pieces is available, not mandatory after a fixed number of words. You may speak a longer sentence when it feels natural. The target is manageable meaning, not sentence counting. A changed, unchanged or uncertain experience is information, not a grade. You do not have to report relief for this attempt to count as exploration.

sections.narration: Use a small structure for one update. Afterwards ask whether the message was understandable and whether you could keep your place. During focused practice, you can deliberately explore this one tool. In an everyday conversation, give most of your attention to the message and the other person. A familiar support can be available if it helps; you do not have to monitor the tool throughout the exchange.
